rejection.expected: The classification rejects the edge; the code uses a type-only import, injected service or shared owner.

recovery.scenario: A disabled Include or later patch means a declared row never mounts.
recovery.expected: The product-use checker counts only effective composition; the package needs a real consumer or classification.

recovery.scenario: An optional bundle list entry is no longer a runtime dependency.
recovery.expected: The gate fails and the list is corrected.

limitations: Static reachability cannot prove a dynamic mount never occurs.
Product-use classification is a policy judgment, not an automatic truth.
The source's specific Cordis/profile representation is product-specific; preserve the classification logic, not the exact paths.
The specific two Agent Teams selections were superseded by a single bundle selection; the installation-owned optional-bundle policy remains.
mechanisms.status: current; optional-bundle policy current, specific Agent Teams selection superseded by one bundle

mechanisms.title: Split artifact production, type checking and the complete build command
mechanisms.problem: A monolithic serial build puts no-emit aggregate type-check programs on the artifact critical path. Developers who need only artifacts must run checks, and there is no command that runs only the checks; the complete build must still detect every type error.
triggers: The build has artifact-producing steps and independent type-check-only programs.
A developer needs artifacts before tests or cold-start, or needs checks before declaring work complete.
A CI job needs a subset of build work.
obligations: Give each command one job: build:artifacts produces every artifact and type-checks package projects; build:check checks only the aggregate root programs; build runs both.
Keep build complete and keep its diagnostics identical to build:check for the aggregate programs.
Do not add prerequisite detection, guards or fallbacks to build:check; let compiler diagnostics (for example missing declaration errors) report missing/stale inputs.
Express steps as a dependency graph with explicit needs; run independent steps concurrently within a configured concurrency limit and topological order when limited to one worker.
Record completion only after every step passes; delete or refuse to write the client build record on any failed or skipped step.
Default local behavior should report all independent failures; use fail-fast only where the source/CI requires it, and propagate outer fail-fast into nested schedulers.
Keep a caller matrix so every command's completeness responsibility is explicit, and do not remove build from required lanes without transferring both checks to another blocking owner.
steps: Separate artifact steps from check-only steps and give each a needs list.
Implement scopes and a complete default in one scheduler; keep commands thin.
Delete obsolete flags and aliases; update every caller.
Verify outputs are byte-identical between serial and concurrent builds and that compiler diagnostic sets match.
Wire required CI lanes to the complete build; record measured trade-offs (memory, CPU, wall).

enforcement.mode: build scheduler plus CI and byte/equivalence evidence
enforcement.implementation: run-gates dependency graph, shell-free spawning, buffered output, process-tree termination, client build record, caller commands in root manifest
enforcement.trust: Byte-identical outputs and compiler dry-run checks prove the tested graph; they do not prove every future caller uses the complete command. Concurrency raises memory and can change scheduling-sensitive behavior.
enforcement.failure: A failed or skipped step exits nonzero and withholds the record; an invalid scope or profile/scope conflict fails argument parsing; a missing prerequisite is a compiler diagnostic, not a green build.
exceptions: Development launch commands and lint/doc prerequisites may intentionally omit aggregate checks; the caller matrix records who owns completeness.
A single-worker mode must still produce identical outputs.

mechanisms.applicability: Repositories with expensive artifact builds plus independent whole-program type checks or other no-emit gates.
relationships: the check-only path can generate declarations without a bundler
scheduling and equivalence measurements
artifacts must be consumed by a strict built-output path

migration.strategy: Extract the no-emit checks from the artifact path, keep a complete aggregate, and migrate callers deliberately.
migration.implementation: Add scopes, a step/needs table, concurrency and fail-fast behavior, record semantics, and byte/equivalence tests; delete old flags.
migration.requiredSupport: A dependency-aware scheduler, reliable process-tree termination, and CI lanes that can run the complete command.

positive.scenario: A root-only test type error is added: artifacts exits 0, check exits nonzero, and the complete build exits nonzero with a partial-step summary and no record.
positive.expected: The commands' responsibilities and record semantics match the documented matrix.

positive.scenario: A concurrent build and a single-worker build produce byte-identical artifacts and compiler dry-run reports no out-of-date project.
positive.expected: The dependency graph is lossless for the tested inputs.

rejection.scenario: build:check silently rebuilds stale prerequisites.
rejection.expected: Review rejects the added work; missing prerequisites remain compiler diagnostics.

rejection.scenario: A failed step still writes the client build record.
rejection.expected: The build is incorrect; the record must be withheld.

rejection.scenario: A caller is left on a removed flag or alias.
rejection.expected: The caller matrix and tests fail; every caller is migrated.

recovery.scenario: Concurrent build exhausts memory.
recovery.expected: Use the single-worker mode or separate artifacts/checks; the trade-off is documented, not hidden.

recovery.scenario: A dependency edge is relaxed without measurement.
recovery.expected: Review rejects the unmeasured change.

limitations: The source's exact TS project layout and measured numbers are project-specific.
Concurrency increases peak memory and contention.
build:check does not detect stale declarations; the caller must rebuild artifacts first.

mechanisms.title: Generate declarations for type checking without bundling
mechanisms.problem: Type-check commands previously ran a full Host bundling pass and Desktop bundle just to obtain Typert declarations. Type checks read package and Typert declarations, not bundler output, so the bundling work sat on the critical path without changing the checked programs.
triggers: A type-check, lint or documentation type-check command needs generated declarations.
A generated declaration writer can run from source without a bundle.
A build command must still generate the same declarations inside the bundler for shipped artifacts.
obligations: Generate declarations for check-only commands with the same generator and writer used by the bundler, but without the bundler or Desktop/Web build.
Make the source-only path fail when a face program loads a workspace package's compiled lib/ output or cannot resolve a workspace import; name the missing source alias.
Run Host source compilation and source-only declaration generation in parallel when the generator reads no build output; make Client compilation depend on both.
Run aggregate checks after their face's package compilation in build mode so they check only the root program and skip current tsbuildinfo.
Keep the complete build path running the same generator inside the bundler; do not move it out for builds when the bundler already overlaps the work.
Document that check-only commands do not refresh runnable bundles and may leave lib/ JavaScript behind declarations.
steps: Identify the declarations checks actually read.
Run source-only generation with the bundler's writer and faces.
Add a build-output guard and source-path alias; test both missing alias and loaded-lib failure.
Order Client compilation after Host source and declaration generation; keep aggregate checks after package compilation.
Compare generated files byte-for-byte with the bundler path and record the known incremental gap.

enforcement.mode: build scope with generator guard plus byte-equivalence tests
enforcement.implementation: generate-typert source pass, shared WorkspaceTypertGenerator/writeWorkspaceArtifacts, rejectBuildOutputs guard, build-mode aggregate checks, build.spec/ generate-typert.spec
enforcement.trust: Byte-identical files and the same checked programs support losslessness; the guard covers workspace lib loads and unresolved imports, not every conceivable build-output read. Incremental declaration invalidation has a known gap.
enforcement.failure: A loaded compiled workspace declaration or unresolved workspace import fails generation with the missing alias; a Typert analysis error fails the step.
exceptions: The bundler plugin may leave rejectBuildOutputs off because it always runs after Host compilation.
Check-only commands intentionally produce no bundle or client build record.

mechanisms.applicability: Type-check or lint commands that depend on generated declarations and currently run a bundler only to produce them.
relationships: check-only scope is one command in the build split
measured local speedup
declarations feed public API catalogs

migration.strategy: Prove the declaration writer can run from source and that no type check reads bundle output, then switch check scopes.
migration.implementation: Add the source-only script, shared writer, build-output guard and source aliases; wire it into typecheck/lint prerequisites; add byte-equivalence and failure tests.
migration.requiredSupport: The generator's source-mode entry point, source path mappings, and a build-mode aggregate check that skips current roots.

positive.scenario: Running the check-only scope with every Typert output deleted regenerates the same 140 files and checks the same programs as the bundler path.
positive.expected: The outputs are byte-identical and the checked program set is unchanged.

positive.scenario: A Host face program resolves a workspace package through exports to lib/ instead of source; generation fails and names the specifier and paths entry.
positive.expected: The guard prevents silent reliance on stale compiled output.

rejection.scenario: The source-only pass runs before Host package compilation and tries to load lib/ declarations.
rejection.expected: The build-output guard fails the step rather than accepting the dependency.

rejection.scenario: A check-only command is expected to produce a runnable bundle.
rejection.expected: The documentation and command contract reject that expectation; run the artifact command first.

rejection.scenario: A Remote declaration changes with no Client source edit and incremental checking misses consumers.
rejection.expected: The known gap is recorded (Issue #6022); the check does not claim to have caught it.

recovery.scenario: The bundler path and source-only path diverge.
recovery.expected: Byte-equivalence tests fail; the shared writer/generator is repaired.

recovery.scenario: A missing source alias appears in a new package.
recovery.expected: Generation fails with the alias remedy; the alias is added.

limitations: Check-only commands leave runnable lib/ output stale until the next artifact build.
Incremental tsc does not record generated Remote declarations reached through exports as consuming-project inputs.
The exact generator and path aliases are product-specific.

mechanisms.title: Lossless gate speedups with measured equivalence
mechanisms.problem: Local hooks and documentation gates spend most wall time on repeated parses, repeated directory walks, serial subprocesses, oversized worker counts and unnecessary bundling. Optimizing by weakening checks or hiding output would trade correctness for speed.
triggers: A local gate, hook or test run is dominated by repeated work rather than unique assertions.
A default worker count comes from host CPUs rather than the actual quota.
A gate performs per-candidate subprocess calls, repeated Markdown parsing or repeated filesystem probes.
A test spends most time on disk-backed fixture setup.
obligations: For every optimization, state measured wall/CPU/memory before and after and prove outputs and diagnostics unchanged, or list the intended behavior difference explicitly.
Measure under representative conditions (shared host/container, CPU quota, load, network filesystem) and report sample count/noise rather than a single best run.
Prefer removing duplicated work: parse each document once, list each directory once, resolve candidates against one object listing, memoize read-only probes, and await real completion signals.
When reusing a parse under normalization, guard the reuse with a proof that the edit cannot change the syntax tree; otherwise fall back to a full parse.
Size local defaults from the actual quota or a measured cap; keep CI behavior explicit and allow override variables.
For in-memory test workspaces, keep the same case names/assertions and document stub and snapshot differences; do not add test-only paths to product source.
Preserve known gaps and trade-offs (memory peaks, stale bundles, stubs, incremental invalidation) rather than claiming full equivalence.
steps: Profile the gate and identify repeated work or an oversized worker pool.
Implement one removal at a time behind the same command and assertions.
Add equivalence tests for byte-identical output, identical file lists and identical diagnostics.
Measure representative runs and record CPU/memory trade-offs and peak memory.
Update contributor documentation for defaults and overrides.
Keep a known-gap list where the optimization cannot preserve a behavior.

enforcement.mode: measurement plus equivalence tests and review
enforcement.implementation: byte-identical output comparisons, seeded-fault equivalence, parse/listing caches, guarded normalization reuse, memoized probes, local parallelism constants, in-memory filesystem test host
enforcement.trust: Equivalence tests cover the tested repository and fixtures, not every future input. Performance measurements are host-specific and noisy. A faster gate that silently drops a file or a diagnostic is a regression, not a success.
enforcement.failure: A changed output, seed failure or missing file fails the equivalence test; an unmeasured speed claim is rejected; a local default above the cap requires an override.
exceptions: A deliberate behavior difference may be accepted when listed (for example skipped unreadable lib directories or stubbed libraries outside one case).
Hosts above the local cap can opt into more parallelism explicitly.

mechanisms.applicability: Local developer gates and CI checks whose runtime is dominated by avoidable repeated work.
relationships: speed must not change the verified predicate
worker limits and teardown interact with contention
build scheduling is one measured optimization

migration.strategy: Profile first, remove the largest repeated work, and prove equivalence before changing defaults.
migration.implementation: Add per-run caches and single-pass APIs, one Git object listing, bounded concurrency with overrides, an in-memory test host, and output-equivalence tests.
migration.requiredSupport: A representative measurement environment, stable fixtures, output snapshots/byte comparisons, and contributor docs for overrides.

positive.scenario: A Markdown link gate parses each file once and reuses the tree; all destinations, anchors and seeded broken links report identically, and wall time falls.
positive.expected: Output is byte-identical and seeded faults behave the same.

positive.scenario: A repository-reference gate lists all Git objects once and binary-searches candidates against it; real and synthetic candidates classify identically to per-candidate lookup.
positive.expected: Classifications match on the full candidate corpus.

rejection.scenario: An optimization skips a file class and a broken link is no longer reported.
rejection.expected: The equivalence test fails; the file discovery is corrected.

rejection.scenario: Local Vitest starts 255 forks on a 64-CPU quota and flakes.
rejection.expected: The cap/override is applied; the uncapped behavior is not accepted as a default.

rejection.scenario: A pairing cache reuses a parse after a link edit that could change the tree.
rejection.expected: The guard falls back to a full parse; unguarded reuse is rejected.

recovery.scenario: A speedup raises memory or leaves stale bundles.
recovery.expected: The trade-off is documented and bounded; callers run the artifact build before using built output.

recovery.scenario: A new gate input class is added.
recovery.expected: The cache/discovery is updated and equivalence tests extend to it.

limitations: Measurements are host- and load-specific.
Equivalence tests cover known fixtures, not every future input.
Some behavior differences (peak memory, stubs, skipped unreadable dirs) remain.

mechanisms.title: Strict built-artifact execution and compile-face test naming
mechanisms.problem: Development-mode tests can run source through tsx and tsconfig path mapping, so they pass even when the built package cannot start under plain Node or resolve its example/config dependencies. Client test files can silently land in the wrong TypeScript aggregate when filenames do not name their compile face.
triggers: CI or a release check boots packaged/example code.
A checked-in Cordis or equivalent configuration resolves bare modules.
A split package has tests for more than one compile face.
obligations: Keep two explicit execution modes: a source/default local mode may use tsx and path mapping; a strict CI mode starts built bins with plain Node and no tsx or tsconfig path mapping.
Run every CI subprocess that boots an example or checked-in config from built lib output; allow source-path tests only as an explicit regression exception.
Place test configurations in the examples workspace member whose node_modules resolves their bare modules, with package-owned fixtures under a predictable group/package path.

Name Client test files by compile face with mutually exclusive suffixes (for example *.client.spec.ts and *.host.spec.ts); let each aggregate use one broad glob and keep helpers/fixtures clearly face-owned.
Verify built binaries and installed/consumer paths, not only workspace source imports.
steps: Build the packages before strict-mode tests.
Launch CI subprocesses with plain Node against built bins.
Place configs and fixtures where upward bare-module resolution finds the intended workspace dependencies.
Classify every Client test by the face it type-checks.
Run the strict suite in CI and record any intentional source-path exception.

enforcement.mode: CI execution mode plus TypeScript project globs
enforcement.implementation: src/lib test modes, plain Node launchers, examples workspace member, face suffixes and aggregate globs, built-bin smoke tests
enforcement.trust: A passing built-bin test proves the tested artifacts start under the CI runtime; it does not prove every published artifact or platform. Face suffixes prove file ownership, not test quality.
enforcement.failure: A built bin that needs tsx/path mapping fails the strict lane; an unclassifiable Client test or wrong aggregate membership fails TypeScript checks.
exceptions: An explicit source-path regression test may remain in src mode.
TypeScript fixtures implementing only a peer protocol without Cordis may run directly with Node.

mechanisms.applicability: Packaged CLIs, plugins and split compile faces where source-mode tests can mask packaging failures.
relationships: artifacts are produced before strict validation
consumer jobs own built-output checks
native jobs must also exercise real process behavior

migration.strategy: Add a strict built-output lane beside source-mode tests, then classify split-face tests by suffix.
migration.implementation: Create src/lib modes, build before tests, use plain Node, centralize example configs under a workspace member, and add face suffixes with aggregate globs.
migration.requiredSupport: A build step in the test job, a workspace examples member, and a TypeScript project layout that can express face ownership.

positive.scenario: A CI subprocess starts a built bin with plain Node and resolves a checked-in config through the examples workspace; it succeeds without tsx.
positive.expected: The packaged path is exercised as a consumer.

positive.scenario: A Host-face Client test is named .host.spec.ts and is included only in the Host aggregate.
positive.expected: Each aggregate owns the correct tests and TypeScript accepts the project references.

rejection.scenario: A built bin only works because tsconfig path mapping is active.
rejection.expected: The strict lane fails; the packaging/path issue is fixed.

rejection.scenario: A Host-face test is left in the Client aggregate.
rejection.expected: The project-reference rule rejects the arrangement; the file is renamed/moved.

rejection.scenario: An example config resolves a bare module from the wrong node_modules.
rejection.expected: Resolution fails or finds an unintended copy; configs are relocated to the owning workspace member.

recovery.scenario: A new split package adds tests.
recovery.expected: The face suffix rule is applied before the aggregates are updated.

recovery.scenario: A source-mode regression is needed.
recovery.expected: It is explicitly marked and does not replace the built-output lane.

limitations: Strict mode still tests only the artifacts built in that job.
Face suffixes are a naming convention and can be misapplied.
Platform-specific process behavior needs native evidence beyond a Node launch.

mechanisms.title: Portable required CI, independent jobs and measured runner policy
mechanisms.problem: A required check can remain queued forever when an org runner pool cannot allocate; job dependencies can put runner availability on the critical path; superseded runs waste capacity; expensive platforms run on every PR without proportional evidence; cache placement and tool provisioning can differ from local behavior.
triggers: A required PR job depends on a special runner pool or a job-level dependency.
A new platform/target is proposed for every PR.
A push supersedes an in-flight run.
A runner pool fails or is reconfigured.
A CI cache or package-manager setup is added.
obligations: Keep required PR verdicts on runners that can actually be allocated; do not assume billing health or a ready runner definition proves a named pool accepts jobs.

Let substantive jobs enter runner allocation independently; remove job-level dependencies that are not true data dependencies, and keep the aggregate verdict dependent only on completed required jobs.

Run the required Windows correctness checks on native windows-build and windows-native-tests; keep windows-coverage outside aggregate needs so it stays visible without delaying the verdict. The Wine PR lane was superseded by native Windows PR CI and now provides post-merge/master toolchain evidence only. When native capacity is unavailable, select a real native failover pool; do not treat Wine as equivalent pre-merge evidence. Portable hosted environments apply only to genuinely platform-independent required checks.
Run expensive platform/target matrices on master only when PR evidence is already covered by the required native surfaces.

Cancel superseded runs per workflow/ref with cancel-in-progress; different PR refs and different workflows do not cancel each other. Exempt release/deployment/metadata and release-owned pack builds because they belong to an intentional publication transaction. Cancellation is a request, not a guarantee of immediate termination. Preserve PR aggregate evaluation after failed/skipped dependencies with !cancelled(), do not upload coverage history for cancelled runs, and retain resource cleanup such as Wine cleanup.
Measure runner size against the actual workload before upgrading; do not buy cores that do not improve the end-to-end gate.
Provision the package manager and caches explicitly and symmetrically; keep CI cache/temp on the intended data disk, not the system disk.
Exercise the trusted self-hosted release rehearsal path when release work depends on it, and preserve fail-loud negative tests.
Keep the local and CI gate entry points on a shared script so behavior does not fork.
steps: List required jobs and their true data dependencies; remove allocation-only serialization.
Choose a portable blocking environment and add independent native jobs.
Configure cancellation and failover, and verify a healthy PR can reach the aggregate.
Measure candidate runner sizes and record wall/cost trade-offs.
Pin tool provisioning and cache paths; verify cold and warm behavior.
Rehearse on the trusted runner and record any residual platform gap.

enforcement.mode: workflow topology, required-check configuration and measured capacity
enforcement.implementation: independent jobs, all-checks-passed aggregate, standard-hosted blocking fallback, native independent jobs, cancel-superseded concurrency, failover variables, pinned package-manager setup, cache/data-disk configuration, self-hosted rehearsal
enforcement.trust: A green workflow proves the jobs that ran; it does not prove a forge branch protection requires them, that a pool will allocate tomorrow, or that a hosted fallback has identical hardware. Runner sizing and caching measurements are environment-specific.
enforcement.failure: A required job that cannot allocate leaves the aggregate pending; a missing dependency or wrong cache path fails visibly; a native-only failure does not silently disappear from required evidence.
exceptions: Advisory native coverage may be non-blocking when the required native build/process checks still run.
Master-only matrices may skip PRs when the required platform evidence is covered.
A failover pool may be selected by an explicit variable.

mechanisms.applicability: Repositories using GitHub Actions or an equivalent with org-owned runners, required checks and platform matrices.
relationships: defines the native checks that CI topology schedules
required verdicts and evidence
contended runners expose flaky budgets

migration.strategy: Make the required verdict portable first, then split independent jobs and move expensive platforms to master.
migration.implementation: Use standard hosted runners for blocking jobs, independent native jobs, an aggregate that only waits on required jobs, cancel-superseded concurrency, explicit tool/cache setup, and measured runner choices.
migration.requiredSupport: Runner inventory and allocation evidence, branch-protection access, cache storage on the intended disk, and failover credentials.

positive.scenario: A healthy PR triggers required substantive jobs that allocate independently and an aggregate that completes; no job waits on an unrelated static build upload.
positive.expected: The PR can satisfy branch protection without a runner-pool deadlock.

positive.scenario: A push supersedes an older run; the older run is cancelled while the current run still produces the required verdict.
positive.expected: Capacity is freed without losing the current evidence.

rejection.scenario: A named org runner pool is unavailable; the required check remains queued.
rejection.expected: The portability failure is visible; blocking jobs must use an allocatable environment or a documented failover.

rejection.scenario: A larger runner is requested without measurement.
rejection.expected: Review requires end-to-end timing/cost evidence; cores alone are not justification.

rejection.scenario: CI cache is placed on the system disk and exhausts it.
rejection.expected: The cache/data-disk configuration is corrected.

recovery.scenario: A failover pool is activated.
recovery.expected: The runbook records the switch, its evidence and the rollback; the trusted rehearsal confirms the production path.

recovery.scenario: A master-only platform hides a PR regression.
recovery.expected: Required native surfaces still cover the behavior; the limitation is explicit, not assumed absent.

limitations: Workflow success is not proof of forge-enforced branch protection.
Hosted and self-hosted runners differ in hardware and trust.
Failure and flakiness can persist; failover and cancellation reduce but do not eliminate queue risk.

A cancelled or still-running standby drill is not failover-readiness evidence; use the latest completed verdict and check its age and commit. Different refs can still compete for shared host capacity, and cancellation latency is not bounded.
The Wine-PR experiment is historical; replaying it as pre-merge Windows evidence would lose the native NT/NTFS/process coverage that superseded it.

mechanisms.title: Native platform evidence beside portable Wine checks
mechanisms.problem: Wine exercises win32 binaries over a Linux kernel, case-sensitive filesystem and hoisted layout; it cannot prove NTFS semantics, DACLs, ConPTY, crash durability or native process behavior. A platform-specific denominator can also hide unsupported source coverage.
triggers: A product supports a native platform whose filesystem, process, permissions or terminal behavior differs from the build host.
A platform-specific lane weakens or narrows the source inventory.
A compatibility layer is used as the only pre-merge evidence.
obligations: Keep portable/Wine checks for post-merge or broad toolchain evidence and add native build/process checks independently for pre-merge correctness.
Run the complete supported source inventory at the same per-file threshold on the native platform; do not shrink the denominator for platform-specific convenience.

Keep blocking native build and targeted native-process checks as required dependencies; place full native coverage outside the required needs so it remains visible and red without delaying the verdict.
Keep observational diagnostics inside the required build job with continue-on-error and fail-fast disabled, so failures are visible but Linux still owns unrelated blocking verdicts.
Disable fail-fast for the diagnostic inventory and give it an explicit timeout; start built-bin smoke only after other observational gates settle.
Preserve separate intentional topologies (portable snapshot vs native immutable workspaces); classify a failure unique to one against its topology instead of weakening or skipping it.
Measure runner size; do not assume more cores improve the end-to-end gate.
steps: Classify which behavior needs native evidence and which is portable.
Run the full inventory at the native threshold, marking only truly platform-specific branches with narrow annotations.
Split blocking build/process checks from coverage and observational diagnostics.
Repair path canonicalization, temp/durability, PATHEXT and process-launch fixtures for the native host.
Measure runner sizes and record which topology each failure belongs to.

enforcement.mode: required native CI plus explicit advisory/coverage lanes
enforcement.implementation: three native jobs (build, coverage, native tests), required needs, continue-on-error observational inventory, per-file coverage threshold, native path/ACL/process fixtures, runner sizing
enforcement.trust: Native execution proves behavior on that host; a green aggregate may still coexist with pending/red native coverage. Observational diagnostics can fail while the PR check remains green, with the failure in step output/summary.
enforcement.failure: A native build or targeted process failure blocks; coverage outside needs stays visibly red; an unsupported-looking file excluded without a narrow annotation is a review finding.
exceptions: Peer-platform-only branches may carry narrow annotated ignores when their behavior is covered on the owning platform.
Full native coverage may be non-required to keep the required verdict fast.

mechanisms.applicability: Products whose supported behavior depends on native filesystem, permissions, process, terminal or addon semantics.
relationships: determines which lanes are required and how runners are sized
native tests need deterministic timing budgets
native jobs exercise built artifacts

migration.strategy: Keep current portable evidence, add one native build and one native process job, then move full coverage outside the required needs.
migration.implementation: Add native jobs with immutable workspaces, full inventory, explicit thresholds, path/process fixtures, observational diagnostics and measured runner sizes.
migration.requiredSupport: Native runner capacity, install/checkout isolation, Developer Mode or equivalent, and a clear blocking/advisory policy.

positive.scenario: A path handling bug caused by an 8.3 alias fails a native test; the fix canonicalizes the existing watch base and the native lane passes.
positive.expected: The native evidence catches behavior Wine did not.

positive.scenario: A PR has green Linux and green required native build/tests while native coverage is red; the coverage failure remains visible and does not fake the aggregate.
positive.expected: The verdict semantics match the documented lane topology.

rejection.scenario: A supported source file is excluded to make the native lane green.
rejection.expected: Review rejects the denominator shrink; only a narrow annotated platform branch is acceptable.

rejection.scenario: An observational diagnostic failure makes the required build job fail.
rejection.expected: The diagnostic must be contained as non-blocking while still visible; blocking build/site steps remain fail-closed.

rejection.scenario: A failure is dismissed as 'Wine-only' or 'native-only' without classification.
rejection.expected: The topology boundary is investigated; the check is not skipped.

recovery.scenario: A larger runner is requested after a 32-core trial improved the gate by only ~1.5s.
recovery.expected: The measurement rejects the upgrade; capacity is not substituted for the actual bottleneck.

recovery.scenario: A native-only crash occurs under contention.
recovery.expected: The fixture uses a real process/exit probe and a bounded budget; the failure is classified against the native topology.

limitations: Native evidence is host-specific and does not prove every supported platform.
Coverage can be red while the aggregate is green.
Observational diagnostics can fail without failing the PR check.
Runner measurements are environment-specific.

mechanisms.title: Release candidate validation, trusted publishing and version identity
mechanisms.problem: Public registries expose uploaded files immediately and cannot replace a filename, so a partially uploaded multi-artifact release can be unusable. Source tests do not prove tarballs contain runtime files. Prerelease identifiers and date-only versions can lose the base release identity or SemVer ordering. Experimental packages may be needed by users without promoting their APIs.
triggers: A release publishes multiple artifacts that must share a version.
A package is experimental but needs installed-consumer access.
A desktop/test build derives a version from a base release.
A release workflow can be run without credentials for validation.
obligations: Validate the complete release candidate without registry credentials: build all target artifacts, download/verify exact filenames and metadata, enforce registry size limits, record SHA-256 and retain one aggregate candidate.
Use trusted publishing/OIDC for the actual publish and grant only repository read permission to validation jobs; a dry run must not be able to enter the publish path.
Verify installed-consumer behavior from packed/extracted artifacts, not only source checkout; include runtime files and imports required by installed consumers.

Publish every intended experimental package in the release family and local baseline while keeping experimental names, opt-in composition, isolation and support limits unchanged; use an explicit denylist for future private exceptions.
Derive a test/prerelease version from the complete base release identity; pass it to packaging as an argument rather than mutating manifests, and do not append a second date suffix.
Keep the distribution feed address independent of version derivation; do not publish the unsuffixed base for a test distribution and disable downgrades for existing clients.
Check existing release records and objects before publishing to avoid duplicate/irreversible uploads.
steps: Build all target artifacts once and assemble the candidate.
Run credential-free validation of filenames, metadata, hashes, size limits and installed-consumer checks.
Keep the candidate immutable and record evidence.
Publish through trusted publishing with minimal permissions and check existing records first.
Derive test versions from the base and document the feed/downgrade policy.

enforcement.mode: release workflow with credential-free candidate validation and trusted publish
enforcement.implementation: candidate artifact assembly, metadata/SHA checks, size limit, installed tarball tests, OIDC publishing, version derivation script, denylist, feed policy
enforcement.trust: Validation proves the candidate's tested artifacts and metadata; it does not prove the registry accepted every file atomically. Trusted publishing proves the workflow identity, not that the version is semantically intended.
enforcement.failure: A mismatched filename/metadata/hash, missing runtime file, oversize artifact or duplicate upload stops the release; validation jobs cannot publish.
exceptions: A future private package may be added to the publication denylist.
A test feed may intentionally not publish the unsuffixed base.

mechanisms.applicability: Any multi-artifact public or private release, especially registries with irreversible uploads and installed-consumer requirements.
relationships: desktop runtime signing is a separate release gate
experimental package publication preserves isolation
notices and metadata derive from the same dependency graph

migration.strategy: Build and validate one immutable candidate without credentials, then add trusted publishing.
migration.implementation: Add a validation workflow, artifact checks, installed-consumer tests, OIDC publish, version derivation and a publication denylist.
migration.requiredSupport: Registry metadata API, artifact storage, OIDC trust configuration and release-record access.

positive.scenario: A release candidate is built for every target, downloaded, checked for exact filenames/metadata/SHA and installed in a consumer; the publish job then uses OIDC.
positive.expected: The candidate is complete and validation cannot publish.

positive.scenario: An experimental package tarball includes its worker runtime file and an installed consumer starts it.
positive.expected: The packed artifact, not only source, is proven usable.

rejection.scenario: A validation job attempts to publish or receives a registry token.
rejection.expected: The permission model rejects it; validation must be credential-free.

rejection.scenario: A test build writes a second date suffix into the manifest.
rejection.expected: Version derivation rejects the double suffix and passes the derived version as an argument.

rejection.scenario: A package is published without checking existing records.
rejection.expected: The release process stops before an irreversible duplicate upload.

recovery.scenario: A release is partially uploaded.
recovery.expected: The registry state is assessed against recorded filenames/hashes; the candidate and missing artifacts guide recovery without claiming atomicity.

recovery.scenario: An experimental package is needed by users but its API remains experimental.
recovery.expected: It is published with unchanged names/isolation and explicit support limits, not promoted.

limitations: Public registry uploads are not atomic; validation reduces but cannot eliminate partial-release risk.
Trusted publishing depends on external identity configuration.
Installed-consumer tests cover the tested platforms and entry points.

mechanisms.title: Signed runtime cache and separate timestamp completion
mechanisms.problem: Rebuilding unsigned native dependencies repeats hardware-token signing and timestamps. A combined SignTool command reports timestamp failure as signing failure; retrying repeats hardware access, while a cached signature can be stale, untrusted or from a different policy.
triggers: A build signs unchanged native/runtime files.
A signing or timestamp operation fails.
A cache entry is restored, published or migrated.
A concurrent build signs the same inputs.
obligations: Cache complete signed runtime files keyed by original content, public certificate, SignTool bytes, signing-script bytes and cache format; retain valid vendor signatures.
Restore only after checking the input record, signed-file digest, Windows trust, timestamp and configured certificate; reject invalid entries without automatic repair or hardware fallback.
Publish complete entries atomically; on concurrent publication keep an existing valid entry rather than overwriting it.

Scope the cache to the current account, a fixed local drive, current-account ownership and a private destination DACL; reject linked/redirected paths and do not treat it as a format for untrusted remote caches.
Serialize each complete signing stage and cache-maintenance operation with an exclusive handle; keep compilation/concurrent preparation outside the lock and recheck after acquisition.
Sign a private PE copy once without a timestamp; release the hardware interlock only after successful execution and verification of the primary signature.

Timestamp fresh copies without signing credentials; retry only on normal failure/warning exits with bounded attempts; launch failure, uncertain termination, storage change or verification failure stops immediately.
Verify Windows trust, timestamp and certificate identity; remove unsigned signature attributes and compare normalized bytes; accept a removal warning only when bytes are unchanged.
Precheck SignTool's longest generated path, use short names in a private directory, journal the mapping, and publish cross-volume copies by hash/recheck/rename then verify committed bytes.
On exhausted attempts, stop packaging/queued work without another hardware call; preserve failure evidence before cleanup.
steps: Compute the cache key from all identity inputs.
Restore to a private staged copy and verify every trust/timestamp/certificate/digest condition.
Acquire the stage lock, recheck, restore hits with a bounded pool, then sign misses serially.
Sign without timestamp, verify primary signature, release the interlock, then timestamp fresh copies with bounded retries.
Publish atomically and verify the committed bytes; retain only valid entries.

enforcement.mode: cache verification, stage locks and signature/timestamp checks
enforcement.implementation: content-addressed signed-file cache, DACL/ownership checks, atomic publish, exclusive Windows handles, signed-PE copy, timestamp retry policy, normalization and path checks, fault tests
enforcement.trust: Verification proves the cached bytes match the configured identity, timestamp and trust state at restore time; it does not authorize clearing a signing interlock or retrying a failed token operation. Cache integrity depends on the build account controlling its files.
enforcement.failure: A corrupt, incomplete, untrusted or incorrectly timestamped entry fails without replacing the target; hardware/primary-verification failure retains the interlock; exhausted timestamp attempts stop packaging.
exceptions: Different timestamp bytes at the same input/policy key need not replace a valid entry; each restore still verifies trust.
A validated explicit cache directory may be used for isolated build storage instead of the profile default.

mechanisms.applicability: Builds that sign native artifacts with hardware tokens and timestamps, especially repeated builds on Windows.
relationships: signed artifacts feed release candidates
bounded workers and locks avoid contention and hangs
packaged runtime paths feed installer/release checks

migration.strategy: Add the cache behind full restore verification, then separate timestamp completion from hardware signing.
migration.implementation: Implement the key and manifest, private staging, stage lock, bounded restore pool, signed-PE copy, timestamp retry policy and fault tests; measure with real hardware callbacks.
migration.requiredSupport: Hardware signing token, trusted Windows verification tools, a local fixed-volume cache location, and an account-scoped DACL.

positive.scenario: A warm build with unchanged runtime files hits the cache, verifies trust/timestamp/certificate, and avoids hardware calls while still running preflight and final artifact signing.
positive.expected: Hardware calls fall and all entries verify; invalid entries fail closed.

positive.scenario: A primary signature succeeds but timestamp fails; the interlock is released and only public timestamp calls are retried up to the bound.
positive.expected: No repeated hardware access; a normal error can recover, an uncertain failure stops.

rejection.scenario: A cache entry's digest or trust check fails.
rejection.expected: Restore fails without replacing the target or falling back to hardware; the entry is not auto-repaired.

rejection.scenario: Two publishers race on the same key.
rejection.expected: One atomic publication wins and the existing valid entry is retained.

rejection.scenario: A timestamp process is terminated uncertainly.
rejection.expected: The retry stops immediately; treating it as a normal failure would risk accepting partial output.

recovery.scenario: The cache is on a redirected/linked path or owned by another account.
recovery.expected: Restore is rejected; the cache must be on a fixed local volume with the right ownership/DACL.

recovery.scenario: A signing stage fails after changing configuration.
recovery.expected: The installer restores the previous value or reports rollback failure alongside the signing failure.

limitations: The cache consumes local disk and depends on account ownership.
It is not a distribution format for untrusted remote caches.
Timestamp service failures remain external and can interrupt a cold build.
Normalization and SignTool behavior are platform-specific.

mechanisms.title: Installer checkout detection, single managed layout and source-plane resolution
mechanisms.problem: A curl|sh installer that always clones creates a second unrelated checkout when run from a real repository. An in-repo direct link cannot be upgraded and can dangle when the checkout moves. A installed source launch can silently fall back to a built lib/ artifact plane when a config specifier lacks a source mapping, so clean checkouts fail while built trees pass.
triggers: The installer runs from stdin or from a checked-out script.
The installer upgrades an existing installation.
A source-mode launch loads a configured package specifier.
A workspace package gains a new subpath used in configuration.
obligations: Detect in-repo execution from the script path ($0): under curl|sh the script arrives on stdin and $0 is the shell; a checked-out copy makes $0 a readable file with scripts/ inside a tree carrying the launcher and install script.
In-repo mode must not clone, fetch, checkout or modify the working tree; it reuses the existing checkout and treats any requested ref as advisory.

Adopt the checkout into the same managed installation layout used by managed installs (staging worktrees plus a stable current pointer); the container owns staging/current, while the repository remains discovered, not owned.
Use one layout for every install; no opt-out that leaves a direct PATH link to a moving checkout.
Resolve every configured local workspace specifier through the source path facade to a .ts/.tsx file; fail when it falls back to a declaration/lib artifact.
Exercise the source launch path in tests, not only a built-lib mode.
steps: Detect stdin versus checked-out execution and set the source root.
Skip clone/update in in-repo mode and adopt the checkout into the managed container.
Point the stable current launcher at the managed layout.
Validate config specifiers against source paths before launch.
Test both source and built execution vectors.

enforcement.mode: installer branch plus config resolution checker and tests
enforcement.implementation: $0-based detection, managed staging worktrees/current pointer, git common-dir discovery, tsconfig paths source facade, verify-cordis-config source-plane check, e2e source launch
enforcement.trust: Detection proves the invocation shape, not the user's intent; source-plane resolution proves a mapped .ts/.tsx exists, not that the module boots. Managed adoption depends on Git worktree behavior.
enforcement.failure: A missing mapping or a fallback to .d.ts/lib fails the config check; a launcher pointing at a moved checkout is a broken install; in-repo mode that modifies the worktree is a defect.
exceptions: The checked-out tree is not owned by the installer and is not cleaned up automatically.
A built-artifact install keeps using the artifact plane separately from source launch.

mechanisms.applicability: Self-installing CLIs that can run from a repository checkout and also manage their own installation.
relationships: both must respect linked worktrees and shared Git state
workspace resolution and path mapping
installed artifacts and consumer checks

migration.strategy: Detect the checkout, stop cloning, then unify the layout and add the source-plane gate.
migration.implementation: Implement $0 detection and managed adoption, add a source-path resolution checker and tests for clean checkouts.
migration.requiredSupport: A shell installer, Git worktree support, tsconfig path mappings and a launcher/current pointer.

positive.scenario: Running scripts/install.sh inside a checkout prints 'using existing checkout', leaves the tree untouched, and adopts it into the managed layout.
positive.expected: No second clone is created and the stable launcher points into staging/current.

positive.scenario: A configured subpath maps to source; the source launch boots. If the mapping is removed, the gate fails naming the specifier.
positive.expected: Source-plane resolution is proven before launch.

rejection.scenario: In-repo mode runs git fetch/checkout or rewrites the working tree.
rejection.expected: The installer behavior is rejected as a violation.

rejection.scenario: A config specifier resolves to lib/prompt.js on a built tree.
rejection.expected: The source-plane check fails; a built tree must not mask a missing source mapping.

rejection.scenario: An install leaves a direct PATH symlink to the checkout.
rejection.expected: Upgrade breaks or dangles; the single managed layout is required.

recovery.scenario: The checkout moves.
recovery.expected: The managed launcher still resolves through the container, not the old path.

recovery.scenario: A new workspace subpath is added.
recovery.expected: Its source mapping is added and the resolution test passes.

limitations: $0 detection depends on shell invocation semantics.
Managed adoption assumes Git worktree/current-pointer behavior.
Source-plane checks cover configured specifiers, not every dynamic import.

mechanisms.title: Worktree-local Git hook installation with ownership and migration guards
mechanisms.problem: Linked worktrees share the common hooks directory, so installing in one worktree can rewrite hooks used by every other. Generated hooks can capture another worktree's binary path; concurrent installs race. A blanket shared-hook change can disable hooks in older worktrees or break custom hook managers.
triggers: A package install runs a hook installer in a repository that may be a linked worktree.
The repository is still Git format 0 and lacks extensions.worktreeConfig.
A hook directory has an ownership marker from a prior install or a copied worktree config.
obligations: Scope hook installation to the current worktree; never remove or rewrite hooks in the common hooks directory.
In CI, return before Git discovery or mutation because automated jobs do not consume contributor hooks.

Require a Git version that can report config scope before changing core.hooksPath; upgrade format 0 only after refusing conflicting direct extensions.*, core.worktree or core.bare values, disabling include expansion, and requiring the common config and every config.worktree to be regular files.

Serialize migration and hook writes with a repository-scoped lock that validates process identity/token/file contents at release; dead or invalid locks require manual recovery, not automatic deletion.

Use an ownership marker for each hook directory and replace only an exact stale owned value after a checkout move; replace a seeded new-worktree config only when it points to a reserved marker-backed hook path of a registered worktree. Before Lefthook runs, require the marker and every generated hook to be an unaliased regular file.
Refuse command-scoped, unowned worktree-scoped and unowned reserved paths; require an explicit override for inherited system/global/common hooks.
On failure after changing core.hooksPath, restore the previous worktree value and report rollback failure alongside the install failure.
steps: Skip in CI; otherwise check Git version and repository format.
Acquire the lock, inspect effective config scope and reject unsafe direct/extension values; disable include expansion and require regular config files.
Upgrade to worktree config, set the worktree-local hooks path, and write the ownership marker.
Run Lefthook; restore the prior value on failure.
Test isolation, copied configs, migration refusals, relocation, concurrency, custom paths and rollback.

enforcement.mode: worktree-scoped installer plus lock and focused tests
enforcement.implementation: extensions.worktreeConfig, per-worktree core.hooksPath, repository lock, ownership markers, inherited-path override, rollback, CI no-op
enforcement.trust: The installer proves it changed only the current worktree's effective hooks under the tested Git behavior; it cannot guarantee a custom hook manager chains them. A lock file's identity check reduces but does not eliminate cross-process races.
enforcement.failure: Conflicting config, unowned paths, stale locks, unsafe migrations or Lefthook failure block installation; rollback failure is reported separately.
exceptions: An explicit environment override may opt the current worktree into an inherited hooks path.
Legacy common hooks remain on disk for unupgraded worktrees and are not auto-removed.

mechanisms.applicability: Repositories using linked worktrees and repo-local Git hooks, especially with automated agents creating short-lived worktrees.
relationships: both discover shared Git state and must not own the checkout
install runs the postinstall hook
local hooks must mirror gate behavior

migration.strategy: Adopt worktree-local hooks through an installer that refuses unsafe shared-config states.
migration.implementation: Add format migration, per-worktree hooks path, lock, ownership marker, override, rollback and concurrency tests.
migration.requiredSupport: Git >=2.26 for --show-scope, Lefthook or equivalent, and linked-worktree test coverage.

positive.scenario: Two linked worktrees install hooks concurrently; each gets its own hooks path and neither changes the other's generated bytes.
positive.expected: Installation is isolated and serialized; repeated installs are idempotent.

positive.scenario: A worktree is moved; its ownership marker allows replacing only the stale owned path.
positive.expected: The new path is installed without overwriting an unowned directory.

rejection.scenario: A format-0 repository has direct extensions.* or core.worktree values.
rejection.expected: The installer refuses migration with a clear diagnostic.

rejection.scenario: A command-scoped or unowned worktree core.hooksPath is present.
rejection.expected: The installer refuses to overwrite it.

rejection.scenario: A dead lock exists.
rejection.expected: Automatic deletion is refused; manual recovery is required.

recovery.scenario: Lefthook fails after core.hooksPath changes.
recovery.expected: The previous value is restored; a rollback failure is reported.

recovery.scenario: CI runs the installer.
recovery.expected: It returns before mutating Git configuration.

limitations: Custom hook managers require explicit integration.
Legacy common hooks can become stale but are not removed.
Behavior depends on Git worktree/config semantics and version.

mechanisms.title: Issue/PR label taxonomy and event-directed lifecycle
mechanisms.problem: Mixing change kind, affected domain and source into one label family makes queries ambiguous. Issue state can drift from review handoffs: an earlier CHANGES_REQUESTED remains effective after a re-request, while a monotonic projection cannot return an automation-owned Issue to In progress. Issue templates and fields can be semantically empty.
triggers: A PR is opened, labeled or reviewed.
An Issue is created/imported into a Project.
A review is requested or changes are requested.
A taxonomy or lifecycle policy migrates labels/fields.
obligations: Every open or merged PR carries exactly one canonical kind/* and at least one materially affected area/*; closed-unmerged PRs keep migrated history without invented classification.
Keep the kind set closed and mutually exclusive; reserve every removed alias so an obsolete synonym cannot reappear as an operational label.

Keep areas extensible by a concise kebab-case name when no honest existing area fits, but never create one for a single PR, incidental path, temporary project, status, person or team; report the addition.
Use native Issue Type for issues rather than duplicating kind/*; source/* records creation only; priority and automation triggers remain independent.
Migrate labels by adding the canonical value, verifying the object, then removing the obsolete assignment; delete a label only when unused.
Treat review webhooks as commands: review_requested -> In review; changes_requested -> In progress; approved/commented submissions do not allocate a runner; dismissed reviews are unsubscribed.
Allow the In review -> In progress backward transition only when the latest target-Project status event was written by the lifecycle actor; a human/unknown actor preserves status.
Keep ordinary PR events forward-only and keep separate policy triggers (for example ready_for_review) with their own owner.

Initialize the organization-level Start date only on pull_request.opened: resolve all same-repository Issue references in the live PR body (resolving and informational), convert created_at to a calendar date in the configured Project time zone, ensure the Issue is a Project item, and write only when the current value is empty. Later events, existing dates and references added after creation are not backfilled or overwritten. Missing configuration fails at policy load; a missing, non-Date or Project-local field, invalid timestamp or API failure fails at the first relevant PR. The mutation has no compare-and-set, so simultaneous PRs can both write the same empty Issue and the last write wins.

Keep Issue templates semantic and minimal: only Bug, Feature and Task; Idea/Research belong in Task unless a future lifecycle decision distinguishes them; frontmatter contains only name, about and type; Markdown headings define hierarchy and HTML comments explain content. The PR template carries Motivation, Changes with adjacent public-interface/behavior placeholders, and Testing entries with proof in a local details element. Policy must not inspect details presentation, visible-body length, title language/prefix or Owner lines, and must not add automatic metadata repair, Issue classification or data migration.
steps: Classify edits into kind and area at PR creation or first review.
Apply the review-command mapping and preserve terminal/human-owned statuses.
Migrate labels with add-verify-remove.
Initialize Start date from pull_request.opened only, using all same-repository Issue references and an empty-value read; do not backfill or overwrite on later events.
Audit invalid Issue labels by direct removal; comment only when the intended value cannot be inferred.
Keep Issue/PR templates semantic and verify their inventory, headings and acceptance of presentation-only differences.
Test the event mapping, runner-allocation condition and human override.

enforcement.mode: label policy plus event-driven workflow tests
enforcement.implementation: label validation, reserved aliases, Project status projection, workflow job conditions, issue templates and policy tests
enforcement.trust: The projection is event-driven and does not repair an event that never runs. ProjectV2 lacks an atomic compare-and-swap between reading the latest status and mutating it. Label checks prove vocabulary, not correct classification.
enforcement.failure: An unsupported kind, missing area, invalid Issue label or wrong review command is corrected/failed; a human-owned status is not overwritten; approved/commented reviews do not consume a lifecycle runner.
exceptions: A repeated review request intentionally moves an automation-owned Issue back to In review even if GitHub reports an older blocking review.
Operational labels may coexist without satisfying kind/area.
A migration may preserve historical assignments on closed-unmerged PRs.

mechanisms.applicability: Repositories using GitHub Issues/Projects and PR reviews as an operational workflow.
relationships: review handoffs and stacked PRs share the review model
policy tests pin the event semantics

migration.strategy: Unify the label vocabulary first, then implement event commands and field initialization.
migration.implementation: Define kind/area, reserve aliases, add Project status projection with actor guard, add issue templates/policy and tests for event mapping and terminal protection.
migration.requiredSupport: GitHub webhooks/Project API, a configured lifecycle actor, and maintainable label descriptions.

positive.scenario: A PR is opened with one kind and two areas; a repeated review request moves an automation-owned Issue to In review, then changes_requested returns it to In progress.
positive.expected: Labels satisfy both dimensions and the two-command projection matches the tests.

positive.scenario: An Issue carries a PR kind label; the lifecycle removes it and reports only an underivable native Type/Priority violation.
positive.expected: Invalid metadata is repaired directly with an audit trail.

rejection.scenario: A human changes the Project status and then a changes_requested review arrives.
rejection.expected: The actor guard preserves the human status; automation does not overwrite it.

rejection.scenario: An approved or commented review attempts to allocate a lifecycle runner.
rejection.expected: The job condition excludes it.

rejection.scenario: A removed alias is recreated as an operational label.
rejection.expected: Policy rejects it; the reserved set prevents the synonym.

recovery.scenario: A review event never runs.
recovery.expected: The projection does not self-heal; replay/repair is explicit and its races are acknowledged.

recovery.scenario: A label migration removes the old value before the new one is verified.
recovery.expected: The migration order is rejected; add-verify-remove is required.

limitations: No scheduled reconciler or atomic compare-and-swap.
Webhook replay can replay an old command.
Label descriptions and issue templates require maintenance.
The source's GitHub-specific behavior must be adapted for other forges.

Only PRs opened after the workflow ships receive Start dates; references added later and existing open PRs are not repaired. The Issue-field mutation has no compare-and-set, so concurrent PRs can race on the same empty Issue and the last write wins.
Policy does not repair legacy metadata, choose missing Issue Types, synchronize Priority or migrate existing data; any such automation needs a separate decision.

mechanisms.title: Official PR stacks, lease-protected refresh and blame-weighted approval
mechanisms.problem: A dependent PR chain represented only by base branches has no official stack identity, so landing requires manual per-PR merges and retargeting. Rewriting reviewed branches can invalidate approvals or checks, yet refusing all rebases blocks the official synchronized workflow. A fixed reviewer weight ignores who authored the changed production code.
triggers: Two or more same-repository PRs depend on each other.
A reviewed branch is rebased, merge-forwarded or synchronized.
A reviewer approval is evaluated for merge.
obligations: Represent every same-repository chain of two or more dependent PRs with the forge's official stack object before landing; treat live stack membership/order as authoritative.

Auto-link an unstacked same-author chain bottom-to-top when authors are known; require explicit confirmation for mixed or unavailable authors, and hard-stop when native stacks are unavailable or the chain crosses forks.
Require user direction before dissolving/rebuilding a conflicting stack or when official order disagrees with branch topology.
Land the complete official stack; a partial landing must name an explicit boundary and merge the bottom prefix; never fall back to per-PR merge plus manual retargeting.
Verify every selected PR independently reaches MERGED before calling the landing complete.
Allow rebase and merge-forward refresh for standalone and stacked PRs, but use an exact lease or lease-protected stack push and abort if the remote moved; never raw-force.
After a synchronized rewrite, validate every rewritten layer before any affected PR merges and re-audit heads, review threads, approvals, mergeability and checks.

For approval weight, compute min(2, 1 + 4 * owned old production lines / total old production lines) from the merge base and blame; do not round before comparing to the two-point threshold; unlinked authors stay in the denominator, additions have no prior owner and contribute no lines to the denominator, and an empty denominator gives no boost.
Mark the approval head pending before dependency setup/history evaluation so an interrupted fetch cannot preserve an earlier approval.
steps: Detect a dependent chain and create/link the official stack with live authors and order.
Refresh history by merge-forward or lease-protected rebase; publish with lease.
Re-audit review state and checks after every rewrite.
Land the whole stack or the explicitly bounded prefix and verify each PR's final state.
Compute reviewer weight from actual changed-line ownership before comparing approval scores.

enforcement.mode: forge stack metadata, lease-protected pushes and approval computation
enforcement.implementation: gh stack link/merge/sync or equivalent, exact leases, post-sync validation, review/check audit, merge-base blame scoring, pending head marker
enforcement.trust: Official stack metadata proves membership/order, not that every layer is correct. Lease protection proves the remote did not move at push time, not that earlier reviews remain valid. Blame scoring proves line ownership, not review quality or independence.
enforcement.failure: Missing native support, cross-fork chains, conflicting membership/order, movement under a lease, incomplete final MERGED state or a lost approval re-audit blocks landing.
exceptions: Merge-forward may be preferred when preserving conflict-resolution checkpoints is more important than linear history.
A same-author legacy chain may be linked automatically; mixed ownership requires a human decision.
Additions have no prior owner and therefore no approval boost.

mechanisms.applicability: Teams using stacked PRs and historical-ownership-based reviewer weighting on a forge with native stack or equivalent metadata.
relationships: review events and merge state feed the workflow
checks and approval evidence are re-audited after rewrites
stack layers should remain independently reviewable

migration.strategy: Adopt official stacks for new chains and lease-protected refresh; add approval weighting only with reliable blame/account linkage.
migration.implementation: Add stack detection/linking, stack landing with final-state verification, lease-protected pushes, post-rewrite audit, and a scoring script using merge-base blame.
migration.requiredSupport: Forge stack API/CLI, branch protection/queue behavior, reviewer account linkage, and a trusted merge-base history.

positive.scenario: A same-author two-PR chain is linked as a stack, landed as a unit, and every selected PR is verified MERGED.
positive.expected: Order and final state come from live stack/PR fields, not local branch inference.

positive.scenario: A 25%-owned production change gives a reviewer the full two-point weight; a 12.5%-owned change gives 1.5 and is not rounded up.
positive.expected: Approval scoring matches the formula and threshold comparison.

rejection.scenario: A mixed-author chain is auto-linked without confirmation.
rejection.expected: The workflow stops and requires a human decision.

rejection.scenario: A stack push moves the remote under a lease.
rejection.expected: The push aborts; raw force is rejected.

rejection.scenario: A post-sync PR merges while local validation is still pending.
rejection.expected: The workflow blocks affected PRs until validation passes.

rejection.scenario: An interrupted history fetch preserves an earlier approval.
rejection.expected: The pending marker prevents the stale approval from being counted.

recovery.scenario: A rewrite invalidates an approval or comment anchor.
recovery.expected: The post-rewrite audit detects it and re-review is required.

recovery.scenario: A conflicting stack membership is found.
recovery.expected: Landing stops for user direction; automation does not dissolve the stack.

limitations: Native stack support and merge queue semantics are forge-specific.
Lease protection does not preserve review validity.
Blame-based weighting depends on account linkage and old-line classification; additions contribute no lines to the denominator and receive no credit.

mechanisms.title: Linter migration parity, staged vs full runs and manual-only expensive workflows
mechanisms.problem: A linter migration can silently lose rules, run a different rule set in pre-commit than in CI, or duplicate formatting in a second tool. Applying overlapping autofixes in one pass can leave newly exposed diagnostics unfixed. Routine translation or dead-code checks can incur orchestration cost far above the work performed.
triggers: A linter/formatter/dead-code tool is replaced or removed.
A pre-commit hook needs a fast subset of a full check.
An autofix invocation reports a non-zero result.
A routine documentation edit needs translation.
obligations: Inventory the old rules and migrate them explicitly; inherited presets or broad categories whose contents may change are not parity evidence.
Keep one authoritative full config and a staged config that inherits it, disables only the expensive analysis, and re-includes files the fast backend cannot analyze.
Use one runner for lint and fix so configuration, startup and dependencies have one boundary.
For fix mode, capture the first invocation; on a completed non-zero result discard obsolete diagnostics, rerun once with inherited output and stop; do not add a second formatter for one pass.
Remove a dead-code or gate tool only after confirming it did not own a unique invariant; record the gate-exception justification.
Make the extended translation/delegation workflow manual-only; routine edits translate the changed content in one pass without generating briefs, delegating or adding a review pass.
steps: Map old rules/checks to the new tool and enable type-aware behavior where needed.
Create the staged config and the single runner; wire hooks/CI to it.
Add a fix retry path for overlapping diagnostics.
Remove superseded tools and update docs/scripts.
Keep expensive workflows behind an explicit command and document the routine path.

enforcement.mode: single runner, parity fixtures and hook configuration
enforcement.implementation: explicit rule config, staged config inheritance, type-aware project discovery, fix retry wrapper, removal of duplicate formatter/dead-code gate, manual-only extended workflow
enforcement.trust: Parity tests prove the mapped rules on fixtures; they do not prove every future rule behavior matches the old tool. Fix retries can still leave semantic issues. Dead-code removal depends on the replacement's coverage.
enforcement.failure: An unmapped rule, wrong staged config, second formatter, non-zero fix result left unreported or a removed gate with an unowned invariant fails review/tests.
exceptions: A staged hook may disable type analysis for speed while inheriting the source rule set.
An extended translation workflow remains available manually for high-risk or large updates.

mechanisms.applicability: Projects migrating developer tooling or tuning pre-commit versus full CI checks.
relationships: the linter is one gate and must not fork local/CI behavior
staged/fast paths and single-runner startup costs
routine translation preserves the pair

migration.strategy: Inventory rules, build one runner with full/staged configs, then remove the old tool and duplicate paths.
migration.implementation: Write explicit configs, a runner with fix retry, parity fixtures, hook wiring and docs; delete the old formatter/dead-code gate after replacement.
migration.requiredSupport: The new linter's rule model and type-aware analysis, fixture coverage for old rules, and a fixer that can rerun on residual diagnostics.

positive.scenario: The staged config inherits the full rule set but disables type analysis; pre-commit runs fast and CI runs the full config; fixtures show no rule loss.
positive.expected: Local and CI use one runner and the intended rule sets.

positive.scenario: A fix invocation exposes a second diagnostic after the first pass; the runner reruns once and reports the final state.
positive.expected: Residual diagnostics are not silently discarded.

rejection.scenario: A migration keeps a broad preset without mapping its rules.
rejection.expected: Parity review rejects it; each rule is explicit or justified.

rejection.scenario: A second formatter is kept to avoid a second fix pass.
rejection.expected: The duplicate config boundary is rejected; one runner owns lint/fix.

rejection.scenario: A routine doc edit auto-invokes the full translation/delegation workflow.
rejection.expected: The routine path is used; the extended workflow is manual-only.

recovery.scenario: A removed dead-code tool was the only owner of a check.
recovery.expected: The invariant is reassigned or the removal is reverted.

recovery.scenario: A fix pass exits non-zero with stale diagnostics.
recovery.expected: The retry path discards them and reruns; a repeated failure is reported.

limitations: Parity fixtures cannot cover every future lint rule.
Staged checks can miss type-aware issues until CI.
Manual-only workflows rely on contributor discipline.
The source's Oxlint specifics may not map to another linter.

mechanisms.title: Design tokens, a living styling specification and recorded deviations
mechanisms.problem: Frontend styling decisions drift between a framework RFC, implementation tokens and component code. Without one living specification, token values, deviation records and review checklists become stale or contradictory; over-tokenizing every value adds ceremony without reuse.
triggers: A web styling framework or token system is introduced or changed.
A component needs a value that differs from the baseline.
A dark-mode, border, elevation or interaction token is added.
A framework-level decision is reconsidered.
obligations: Keep the framework decision in an RFC (rarely changing) and the authoritative token values, coding checklist and deviation record in a living specification.
Send token/new-rule changes to the living specification; overturning the framework requires a superseding RFC.
Start from the surveyed visual baseline; allow a deviation only when it is recorded in the deviation table (date, item, reason) before landing code.

The archived note's two-layer --bg-*/--text-* token table and global.css home were superseded by the 2026-07-22 --dsw-* static+alias sheets. Keep the framework rulings (CSS Modules + clsx, no component library, no Tailwind, tokens-only colors) but use the current living token source; do not copy the retired table or add a third layer without need.

Do not tokenize font sizes and spacing by default (the source used px with paired line heights and a 4-multiple spacing scale); treat the specific names, layers and scope as current-living-spec data, and do not force the source table onto a target with a different token system.

Read borders, interaction and dark-mode rules from the current living spec; keep the source principle of a single dark-mode override rather than scattered overrides, but do not derive implementation from the retired --bg-*/--text-* table.
steps: Record the framework decision and the visual baseline survey.
Use the current living token system (for example static+alias sheets), not the archived two-layer table; record deviations before implementation.
Record deviations before implementation.
Review new components against the checklist and token table.
Supersede the RFC only for a framework-level change.

enforcement.mode: living specification, review checklist and deviation record
enforcement.implementation: docs/web-styling spec, semantic token table, checklist, deviation table, RFC status
enforcement.trust: The spec proves recorded values and deviations; it does not prove visual quality or accessibility. Code review still checks actual usage.
enforcement.failure: An unrecorded deviation, a new token not in the spec, or a contradictory RFC/living spec is a review finding.
exceptions: A recorded deviation may depart from the baseline for a stated reason.
Font sizes/spacing may remain literal when tokenization adds no reuse.

mechanisms.applicability: Web UI projects with repeated visual tokens and a need to distinguish stable framework decisions from evolving values.
relationships: RFC versus living-spec ownership
deviation records and checklists make review decidable
documentation contract for frontend guidance

migration.strategy: Write the living spec and baseline tokens before enforcing a checklist.
migration.implementation: Record the survey, token layers, deviation table and checklist; point component reviews at them; keep the RFC separate.
migration.requiredSupport: Frontend code review, a documentation location, and agreement on the visual baseline.

positive.scenario: A component adds a spacing value on the 4-multiple scale with the paired line height and no new token.
positive.expected: It matches the living spec and needs no deviation.

positive.scenario: A deliberate deviation is recorded with date/item/reason before code lands.
positive.expected: The deviation table and code agree.

rejection.scenario: A component invents a new semantic token outside the table.
rejection.expected: Review requires a living-spec change or reuse of an existing token.

rejection.scenario: A framework-level change edits only the living spec.
rejection.expected: The change requires a superseding RFC.

rejection.scenario: Dark mode is implemented with scattered component overrides.
